1.pericope_label: The maimed and the eunuch shut out of the congregation

schools.summary: Gill reads the wound as deliberate, not accidental — crushed by the hands of men with design to unfit a man for generation or make a eunuch of him. Calvin refuses both the common readings of what entering the congregation means, calling them tame: the point is not admission to office nor to citizenship but exclusion from the sacrifices and the solemn assemblies, so that the bar is a religious one and the punishment falls where it will be felt.

Henry lays out three readings of the phrase, the third from Bishop Patrick, and does not force a choice among them. He balances the severity with the promise of Isaiah, where the eunuch who keeps the sabbath is given a name better than of sons and daughters, so that what the law shut out the gospel takes in.

Clarke and Wesley both take the exclusion to be from civil office and honour rather than from worship, Wesley arguing the point from the word Kahal, which he takes to denote the assembly of the rulers rather than the body of the people. Clarke adds that the mutilations in view were pagan and self-inflicted.

Keil sets the law in the chapter's structure, reading the whole as a series on who may and may not be received. Ellicott brings the Isaiah counterweight forward and notes the contrast with Galatians, where Paul turns the language of mutilation against those who would compel circumcision.

debates.question: From what exactly were the maimed excluded?

positions.position: from civil office and public honour, not from worship
from the sacrifices and solemn assemblies — a religious exclusion
the phrase admits more than one sense and need not be settled

outliers.note: calls both the usual explanations tame and insists the exclusion is from the sacrifices themselves

themes: what entering the congregation of the Lord means
mutilation and the bar to the assembly
the Isaiah 56 counterweight

2.pericope_label: The bastard, Ammon and Moab, Edom and Egypt

schools.summary: Gill reports the common Jewish reading of the word for bastard, gathered from its place immediately after the incests of the preceding chapter, and passes on the rabbinic view that the law was framed to deter, adulterers seeing they fix an irreparable stain on their family. He also records the limitation of the Ammonite rule to men, the children following the father. Calvin distinguishes two senses and approves the narrower, but flatly refuses to let the shame fall on the child as guilt: God did not shut these unhappy persons out of the hope of salvation, but humbled them by a temporal punishment. On Ammon and Moab he denies the incestuous origin has anything to do with it, presses the aggravation that as Lot's descendants they should have owned Abraham's children as brethren, and reads the hiring of Balaam as an attempt to overwhelm God by magical incantation. The leniency to Edom and Egypt he cannot fully explain, and rests in God's free right to chastise the same sins more lightly in some than in others.

Clarke glosses the word briefly as one born in incest or adultery, and observes that the bar on Moab did not disqualify from proselytism, since Ruth married Boaz and became a progenitor of our Lord. Wesley draws the lesson from Egypt: thou wast a stranger and didst receive habitation, protection and provision a long time, and that kindness is not to be forgotten for the persecution that followed, since with men one injury blots out the memory of twenty courtesies, but God does not deal so with us.

Keil denies the word covers illegitimate children generally, as the Greek and Latin versions took it, holding with the Talmud that it means those begotten in incest or adultery, and finds in the tenth generation the number of complete exclusion rather than an absolute bar. Against Knobel he insists Ammon and Moab were shut out for their hostility to God's kingdom, not for their forefathers' incest. Ellicott records the same rabbinic limitation to men and adds Rashi's contrast, that he who makes a man sin treats him worse than he who kills him.

debates.question: Why were Ammon and Moab shut out?

positions.position: for their hostility to Israel — the bread and water withheld, and Balaam hired — not for their incestuous descent

debates.question: How wide is the term rendered bastard?

positions.position: narrow — those begotten in incest or adultery, as the Talmud holds
two senses are current; the narrower, of children born of gross prostitution, is to be preferred

outliers.note: refuses to treat the child's shame as guilt, and confesses he can find no reason for Edom's lighter sentence but God's free will

9.pericope_label: Keep thee from every wicked thing: the purity of the camp

schools.summary: Gill glosses the marching host briefly. Calvin makes the verse an argument against excuses: what was taught of purity at home and in peace is extended to the clang of arms, because laws are disregarded in war, when violence rules instead of reason, and soldiers are granted a licence not tolerated otherwise. God removes the plea by requiring the same purity in both. From this Calvin draws the general rule that empty excuses for breaking God's commands are worthless — however hard the duty, God never resigns his rights — and turns it round: if war, which seems to suspend all law, excuses no crime, far heavier is the guilt of those who pollute themselves in peace with quiet minds. On the covering of excrement he answers the scoffers who think the smell was said to offend God's nostrils, holding that such rudiments kept the people to their duty, since licence in trifles leads on to audacity, and denying it was merely sanitary.

Henry reduces the passage to one word — be clean — and divides the pollutions into moral, ceremonial and natural. On the first, sin takes off the edge of valour and guilt makes men cowards; those who carry their lives in their hands need a conscience void of offence, and must not gratify malice, covetousness or uncleanness under cover of a commission, nor keep the accursed things of the camps they plunder. Those who stayed at home were bound too, lest their sin drive God from the army; times of war should be times of reformation. On the second he notes that the soldier is bound more strictly than the man at home, who need only wash, while the soldier must withdraw from the camp ashamed of his own impurity.

Wesley gives three compact reasons for the charge: war is a season of confusion and licence, when the laws of God and man cannot be heard for the noise of arms; success depends on a blessing wicked men have no reason to expect; and a man with his life in his hand had need be ready for death and judgment. Clarke declines to think the sanitary directions trifling — decency and cleanliness promote health and prevent disease.

Keil marks a tightening of the earlier rule: on the desert march only lasting uncleannesses put a man outside the camp, but in an encampment even a night's defilement does, until he has washed at evening and the sun is down. On the covering of excrement he is exact — there was nothing shameful in the thing itself, but the irreverence of leaving it would offend the Lord who walked in the midst, and drive him from the camp.

debates.question: Why is so small a matter as covering excrement given a place among God's laws?

positions.position: to hold the people to duty in trifles, lest licence there lead on to audacity — not for health, and not because the smell offends God
because the irreverence of leaving it, not the thing itself, would drive the Lord from the camp
decency and cleanliness promote health and prevent disease

outliers.note: argues a fortiori that guilt is heavier in peace than in war, since war at least offers the pretext of necessity

themes: why war does not suspend the law of purity
the three pollutions of the camp
the reason given: God walks in the midst

15.pericope_label: Thou shalt not deliver the escaped servant to his master

schools.summary: Gill supplies the clause the words omit: the servant meant is one used ill by a tyrannical master, in danger of his life or of being maimed. He is not to be bound and sent back but kept until the master's anger subsides or the quarrel is inquired into, and it cannot be thought the law protects every idle and disobedient servant. Gill reports the Jewish reading, with Onkelos, of servants of idolaters fleeing for religion. Calvin states the difficulty at length before answering it: the refuge as worded defrauds masters of their right, violates the law of nations, and would fill the land with criminals — a thief or murderer sheltered there would overthrow justice. He therefore holds more is meant than the words express, infers from the choice of city that judicial proceedings were held, and files the law under the sixth commandment, as forbidding the people to become accessory to another's cruelty.

Henry makes the land a sanctuary for wronged servants, with the same caution — Israel did not need, as Rome at first did, to be peopled by unprincipled men. The trembling servant is not handed over until trial shows he wronged his master; the angel sent Hagar back and Paul sent Onesimus, neither being in danger, but this man runs for his life, and to give him up is to throw a lamb into the mouth of a lion. Once the abuse is proved, protection is not enough: he must be encouraged to settle where it likes him best, neither imposed upon nor trading one hard master for many, since converts deserve particular tenderness lest they be tempted back.

Clarke restricts the case flatly to a servant leaving an idolatrous master to join God's people, since otherwise it would be injustice to harbour a runaway. Wesley argues from distance that the master must be a near neighbour, a man being unlikely to flee so far or a master to pursue so far, and grounds the ruling in God's own sovereign right over both parties, adding that it is not strange the God who hates tyranny and calls himself the refuge of the oppressed should interpose.
Keil reads it of a slave fled from abroad because of harsh treatment by a heathen owner, and pairs it with the next law as toleration set against non-toleration in the congregation.

debates.question: Does the law shelter any runaway at all?

positions.position: no — only one fleeing an idolatrous master for religion

one fled from harsh treatment by a heathen master abroad

16.pericope_label: No prostitute in Israel, no hire in the house, no usury of a brother

schools.summary: Gill takes the provision for the fugitive's dwelling as confirming that a proselyte servant is meant, and dwells on the strangeness of the Hebrew word for prostitute, which properly means a holy one and here by contrary usage an impure one; Jarchi glosses it of a woman who separates herself for the trade and then makes herself common, and Gill cites Strabo on the thousand sacred harlots kept at the temple of Venus in Corinth, with a like multitude at Comana. On usury he explains that Israel farmed rather than traded, so borrowed only for subsistence and could not bear interest, while the merchant stranger gained by what he borrowed. Calvin is less confident of the etymology and leaves the masculine term open between catamite and mere fornicator, citing Job; he notes that a pig's price might be offered though a dog's might not, so the dog is rejected as vile and contemptible rather than merely unclean; and he turns the usury law into a positive duty, since liberality is a part of righteousness and he is unrighteous who will not relieve his brethren when he can.

Clarke observes that public prostitutes commonly dedicated part of their earnings to their gods, some being kept in the temple of Venus Melytta with their gains applied to that worship. Wesley reads the prohibition as aimed at the Gentile practice of using prostitution in worship, forbidden to Israelites in a peculiar manner as far more odious in them; he takes the price of a dog for a whoremonger's takings, dogs being so called in the Revelation; and on usury he explains that the lender lost little, estates being settled and merchandise rare, while it is just that the trading stranger should share his gain with the lender.

Keil insists the point is cultic: what was forbidden was that an Israelite should give himself up to prostitution as an act of worship, foreign prostitutes being already excluded by the command to root out the Canaanites, and the two words naming those who prostituted themselves in the service of Astarte. He reads the refusal of the wages as extending to the persons themselves, both being an abomination. Ellicott agrees that both terms belong to the temples of Baal and Ashtaroth, and presses the second clause: a lamb or kid might not be sacrificed if it came as the wages of sin, and while an ass could be redeemed with a lamb, the dog admits no such exchange.

debates.question: Is the prohibition aimed at prostitution generally or at its cultic form?

positions.position: at the cultic form — prostitution as an act of worship
a general precept of chastity, whatever the etymology of the word

outliers.note: notices that a pig's price might be offered though a dog's might not, and concludes the dog is refused as contemptible rather than merely unclean

themes: the sacred prostitutes of Canaan

21.pericope_label: Vows: bound if made, no sin if withheld

schools.summary: Gill limits what may be vowed to what is in a man's power, lawful and agreeable to God's revealed will — a sacrifice beyond the required, a gift toward the sanctuary or the poor — and marks the release in the following verse, that a man of means might forbear to vow without guilt, though freewill offerings proportioned to his ability were expected. Calvin files vowing under the third commandment, since a vow is a covenant contracted with God himself, and holds that the vows which pleased God were testimonies of gratitude used as a spur to slow thankfulness. Against those who would keep every vow whatever, he insists a definition must come first: if all rash promises bound, it would once have been right to kill sons and daughters and raise altars to idols. Nothing may be vowed but what pleases God, and since nothing is to be done without faith, even indifferent things may be vowed superstitiously. Breach is doubly guilty because silence was open, as Peter told Ananias the field was his own; and the phrase gone out of thy lips is no ceremony but a curb, a vow being complete only when heart and tongue agree.

Wesley reads not slack as not delay, since delay makes a man both unable and unwilling to pay, and states the residue of the third verse exactly: the offering was free while unmade, but once made a man is no longer free.

Ellicott notes that Rashi and the rabbis make the three yearly feasts the occasions for payment, and that Ecclesiastes takes the precept up with enough verbal difference that it cannot be called a quotation.

debates.question: Must every vow be kept, because whatever passes the lips must be paid?

positions.position: no — only vows of things lawful and pleasing to God; the unqualified rule would have justified killing children and raising altars to idols

outliers.note: reads the release from vowing as an indirect lesson in restraint, since those who plunge in either repent at once or pay in a servile temper that destroys the grace of the act

themes: a vow as a covenant contracted with God
which vows bind and which do not
the release: forbearing to vow is no sin

24.pericope_label: Grapes at pleasure, ears by hand: no vessel and no sickle

schools.summary: Gill pictures the vineyard visit and the road running through standing corn, as when Christ and his disciples went through the grain; the ears are plucked, rubbed to loose the grain from husk and beard, and eaten to satisfy hunger, while bringing a sickle to cut and carry off would be simple injustice. He reports that Jarchi and the Targum of Jonathan read the second case of a hired workman taking wages in kind, but prefers the plainer sense. Calvin knows the same restriction to harvest labourers from the Chaldee and rejects it: the concession is to all persons and grants no more licence than humanity demands. His argument is from the Lawgiver's intention — if a man plucked with bare hands all the ears he could carry on his shoulders or load on a horse, would the absence of a sickle excuse him? Since common sense repudiates that, the law's object must be that no one touch even an ear except for present use, as the disciples did when hunger drove them. A man who breaks into a vineyard and gorges himself is a thief whatever he pleads, and vineyards were hedged and guarded; what is permitted is that hungry travellers without other food refresh themselves until they reach a lodging where bread and wine can be bought.

Wesley explains the liberty of eating at pleasure by the great plenty and fruitfulness of vines in those parts. Clarke draws the moral of both verses: it was on the permission granted by this law that the disciples plucked the ears, and the statute is a considerate and humane one, no dishonour to the Jewish code.

Keil states the principle behind both clauses — a passer-by might eat at pleasure to still his hunger but carry off no store of grapes or ears — and observes that the right of hungry travellers to pluck, rub out and eat as they cross a field is still recognised among the Arabs. Ellicott meets Rashi's attempt to confine both precepts to the labourer gathering vintage or harvest, when vessels and sickles are in use, and holds the plain meaning stands, since our Lord accepts it: the objection raised against the disciples was not that they plucked their neighbour's corn but that they did it on the Sabbath, plucking counting with the scribes as a kind of harvesting.

debates.question: Rashi, the Chaldee and the Hebrews generally confine these permissions to hired labourers gathering the vintage or harvest. Does that restriction hold?

positions.position: no — the plain sense stands, the concession is to any passer-by, and our Lord accepts it so

outliers.note: tests the letter of the law by reductio — a man loading a horse with hand-plucked ears keeps the words and breaks the intention

themes: the two liberties and their limits
whether the law concerns labourers or all passers-by
the disciples in the cornfield
